newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Peru rebels say they won't harm hostages.
newsitem.headline: Peru rebels say they won't harm hostages.

text.p: Marxist rebels holding 73 hostages at the Japanese ambassador's residence in Peru will not hurt any of their captives, a rebel spokesman said on Tuesday.

"Under no circumstances will we act aggressively against (the hostages), whether verbally or physically," Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) spokesman Isaac Velazco told a news conference in Stockholm.

"We see them as prisoners of war and we treat them according to the valid regulations (the Geneva convention). Unless the regime attacks the residence and kills all of the commando, we will respect their status as prisoners of war."
The MRTA has been holding 73 hostages since taking over the ambassador's residence on December 17 during a cocktail party.
During the raid the rebels took hundreds of guests captive but most were later released.
The MRTA is calling on Peru's President Alberto Fujimori to release political prisoners, among them MRTA members, to improve prison conditions and to end free market policies.

Velazco said he was in Sweden to spread information about the situation in Peru and to call for "progressive" people's solidarity to support a political solution to end the 35-day stand-off between the Peruvian government and the MRTA.
He said his visit had nothing to do with rumours a few weeks ago that guerillas holed in at the residence might want to seek political asylum in Sweden.

"Fujimori's government has attempted to confuse the international opinion by spreading information about commando members being prepared to seek asylum in different European countries," Velazco said through a translator.
He said guerrillas could have fled the country already if they had wanted to.
Velazco, who is based in Germany, said the MRTA's original demands were still valid.
A pledge from Fujimori about treating prisoners according to international conventions was not sufficient.
"We never believe in promises from tyrants and dictators," he said.
Responding to criticism that the group lacked popular support, he said people were just waiting to see what would happen, neither supporting Fujimori nor fully backing the MRTA.
"Fujimori has been badly hurt by what has happened and is standing with his back against the wall and the people know that," Velazco said.
"But they also know that Fujimori controls the security organisation and the army."
